## February 29, 1960 — A Monday

You arrived on a day that doesn't exist most years.

February 29 comes only every four years, which means you share your exact birthdate with a rare cohort — people who have celebrated sixteen recurring "official" birthdays while growing sixty-six years older. In the years when the calendar skips your date, the question of when to mark the occasion has no clean answer. You have lived a full life on a partial calendar.

The world you entered was itself at an unusual hinge point — not the middle of a decade but its very first year, a year historians would come to call the threshold between the postwar order and everything that followed.

---

**On the exact day you were born**, the Agadir earthquake had just struck Morocco.

At 11:40 at night on February 29, the city of Agadir collapsed in fifteen seconds. An estimated 12,000 to 15,000 people died — roughly a third of the city's entire population — as buildings fell in the dark while residents slept. It was one of the deadliest earthquakes of the twentieth century measured by the fraction of a community destroyed. You were born into the hours after one of the worst single nights in Morocco's modern history, on the same calendar day.

1960 was also the "Year of Africa." Seventeen African nations gained independence that year, as the British and French empires shed colonies at a pace that would have been unthinkable five years earlier. The map of the world was being redrawn in the months around your birth, continent by continent, faster than newspapers could keep up.

Dwight Eisenhower was in the final year of his presidency. A young senator from Massachusetts named John Kennedy was beginning to build a campaign that would transform American politics — and, for a brief and complicated moment, American hope.

---

**Within thirty days of your birth — one historically significant worldwide event:**

On March 21, 1960 — twenty-one days after you were born — South African police opened fire on a crowd of Black protesters in Sharpeville who were demonstrating against the pass laws. Sixty-nine people were killed, most of them shot in the back as they fled. The Sharpeville Massacre shocked the world in a way that apartheid's daily brutalities had not quite managed to do. It triggered international condemnation across dozens of countries, led to South Africa's eventual expulsion from the Commonwealth, and lit the fuse under the international anti-apartheid movement that would burn for thirty more years. The world you were born into was beginning to argue, seriously and at last, about whether racial subjugation anywhere was the rest of the world's business.

---

**The arc of your sixty-six years:**

You were three years old when Kennedy was shot in Dallas. You were nine when Armstrong walked on the moon. In both cases old enough to know something enormous had happened, but not quite old enough to carry it as fully conscious political memory. That is the precise developmental circumstance of the 1960 cohort: too young to own the 1960s as lived experience, old enough to be shaped entirely by their aftermath.

You were fourteen when Nixon resigned and the country's relationship with its own institutions became permanently more suspicious. Nineteen when the Iranian Revolution remade the Middle East and American hostages were taken in Tehran. Twenty when Reagan was elected and the country turned sharply in a new direction.

You were twenty-nine when the Berlin Wall fell — exactly the right age to understand what that meant. Your entire childhood had been organized around the Cold War as permanent fact. By twenty-nine you had internalized all of it, and you were young enough to watch it dissolve and feel, for a real moment, that history had shifted on its axis.

You were forty-one on September 11, 2001. Forty-eight when the financial system nearly collapsed. Fifty-nine when the pandemic arrived. Sixty-six now, in the first years of artificial intelligence as a mass cultural force, still watching history shift.

---

**The world you entered, the world you inhabit:**

You were born into a world of roughly three billion people. Jet passenger travel was new enough that crossing the Atlantic still felt like an event. The contraceptive pill had not yet been approved by the FDA — that came two months after your birth, in May 1960. The first working laser was demonstrated that same month. Television was becoming universal, but it was black-and-white and broadcast on three channels.

You are sixty-six years old in a world of eight billion. The seventeen African nations that gained independence in your birth year are older than you are. The apartheid system that killed sixty-nine people in Sharpeville when you were three weeks old ended in 1994, when you were thirty-four. The Cold War that organized your entire childhood dissolved when you were twenty-nine, on a November night in Berlin.

And you share your birthday with a very small number of people. Every four years the calendar catches up, and the date that existed when you arrived comes around again. There is something fitting about that — being born on a day the world mostly skips, in a year when the world was changing faster than it had in many that came before it.
